newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban suffer setback as opponents organise.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban suffer setback as opponents organise.

text.p: Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban said on Wednesday they had halted a fierce counter-attack from ousted government army chief Ahmad Shah Masood, but they clearly suffered a serious military setback.

Western aid workers quoted witnesses in the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush mountains, as saying they had seen at least 100 bodies of Taleban fighters and many more wounded being ferried down the steep-sided, narrow pass since the fighting began on Tuesday.
"One counted 39 bodies being brought down in just one hour," one said.
Maulavi Khairulla Haqani, the Taleban battlefield commander in the Salang, told Reuters Television the fighting had been fierce.

"It was very hard to contain the attacks and the fighting was very serious, but we brought up heavy reinforcements and halted it. We are now in control," he told correspondent Laurent Hamida on the front line.

But his new command post was 15 to 20 km (nine to 12 miles) south of where the Taleban front line had been in the Salang Pass, a winding defile that runs north from Kabul to Mazar-i-Sharif, headquarters of Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum.

Dostum appears to be moving to join Masood but in Kabul, the Taleban leadership dismissed the potency of any such alliance after ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani met Dostum in Mazar-i-Sharif on Tuesday.

"Rabbani is at the end of things. He is going to be finished very soon along with his forces, so I don't think Dostum will get together with him at this stage," acting deputy foreign minister Sher Mohammed Stanakzai told a news conference.

The Taleban say they are dedicated to bringing peace, security and the stern Islamic Sharia law to Afghanistan, ravaged by 17 years of war, and that they want all Afghans to take part in a future government without ethnic considerations.

Stanakzai repeated the position of the Taleban, the movement founded by religious students which captured Kabul on September 27 and swept north to bottle up Masood in his Panjsher Valley fortress, that they would rather negotiate with Dostum than fight him.

But Dostum told reporters in Mazar-i-Sharif, from which he controls six of Afghanistan's 33 provinces with a strong army and small air force, that Masood, an ethnic Tajik, was due in the city on Wednesday or Thursday.
That was a strong signal of an imminent political alliance and the Salang Pass fighting suggested that cooperation on the ground was already in place.

Haqani said Tuesday's attack was launched by Basir Solangi, Masood's commander in the pass, who withdrew into Dostum territory as the Taleban drove north and who was described by an Uzbek general last week as Dostum's "honoured guest".
"An honoured guest does not start a battle without the approval of the host," said one veteran Afghan watcher in Kabul.
Solangi's attack forced the Taleban to suspend the assault on the Panjsher from the town of Golbahar, which sits astride the sheer-sided gorge that leads into it.
"There are no Taleban left in Golbahar. They've all been switched to the Salang," one aid worker quoted witnesses as saying.
The aid workers said the Taleban had suffered some 270 casualties, many of them from landmines, since they began their attempt to break into the Panjsher on Saturday.
By the time they broke off the attempt, they had managed to push only a short way into the gorge.
In the Salang, Taleban fighters said on Tuesday Solgani's men had come through the pass and over the mountainsides to launch their assault.

The aid workers said Solangi had cut the road well south of the Taleban front line and isolated a large body of the Islamic militants and cut them to pieces with mortars, heavy machine guns and artillery.
Haqani, however, said no heavy weapons were used apart from two tanks and that he did not know whether these belonged to Masood or Dostum.
Dostum, a communist general who switched sides in 1992 shortly before Islamic guerrillas won Kabul after 13 years of fighting a Soviet-backed regime, was then a Masood ally.

They split two years later and Dostum withdrew to Mazar-i-Sharif, and are still far from friends. But Dostum, who presides over a very liberal Islamic regime, seems to have decided the Taleban are the main enemy, Afghan watchers said.
"It appears we are entering a new phase of the war," one said.
